title: THE KING WHO CUT GOD’S WORD WITH A KNIFE AND BURNED IT
paragraphs: THE KING WHO CUT GOD’S WORD WITH A KNIFE AND BURNED IT
He thought destroying the scroll would silence the warning. Instead, God rewrote the words—and history remembered the man who tried to burn them.
There is something terrifying about watching a man hold the Word of God in his hands…
and reach for a knife.
Not because he misunderstood it.
Not because he could not read it.
Not because nobody had warned him.
But because he understood enough to know that he did not want to hear it.
His name was Jehoiakim.
He was king of Judah.
He had a palace, servants, authority, wealth, political power, and a throne inherited from a dynasty whose story stretched back to David.
But one winter day, while sitting comfortably beside a fire, this king was confronted by something more powerful than his throne.
The Word of God.
And when the Word began exposing what he did not want exposed, Jehoiakim did something almost unimaginable.
He took a knife to it.
Then he threw it into the fire.
And perhaps that is why his story is so uncomfortable.
Because most of us have never physically burned a Bible.
But some of us have become very skilled at cutting out the parts we do not want to obey.
Stay with this story.
Because before it is over, the knife in Jehoiakim’s hand may begin to look disturbingly familiar.
The account is found in Jeremiah 36.
Judah was living under the shadow of judgment. The nation had repeatedly rebelled against God, and Jeremiah had spent years proclaiming warnings that were anything but comfortable.
Then the LORD commanded Jeremiah to take a scroll and write upon it the words He had spoken concerning Israel, Judah, and the nations.
And God revealed something beautiful about the purpose behind the warning.
Jeremiah 36:3 records:
“Perhaps the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
That matters.
God was not warning them because He delighted in destruction.
The warning itself was mercy.
Behind the announcement of judgment stood an invitation to repentance.
Behind the frightening words stood the possibility of forgiveness.
In the Hebrew text, the heart of the invitation is:
וְיָשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ מִדַּרְכּוֹ הָרָעָה
veyashuvu ish middarko hara'ah
“…that each man may turn from his evil way…”
Then comes the breathtaking purpose:
וְסָלַחְתִּי לַעֲוֹנָם וּלְחַטָּאתָם
vesalachtî la'avonam ulechatatam
“…and I will forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
The Hebrew verb behind “turn,” שׁוּב — shuv, carries the basic idea of turning or returning.
That is the heartbeat of biblical repentance.
Turn.
Come back.
Stop running toward destruction.
Return to the God you abandoned.
And notice what waits on the other side.
Forgiveness.
The God who exposes sin is also the God who offers mercy to sinners who turn to Him.
So Jeremiah dictated the message to Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote the words upon a scroll.
Eventually that scroll reached the royal court.
Jehudi began reading it aloud before King Jehoiakim.
Picture the room.
It was winter.
The king was sitting in his winter apartment.
A fire burned before him.
The scroll was being read.
The words of God were entering the room sentence by sentence.
Then Jeremiah 36:23 tells us what happened:
“When Jehudi had read three or four columns, the king cut them off with a scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire in the brazier, until the entire scroll was consumed in the fire.”
Three or four columns.
Slice.
Fire.
More words.
Slice.
Fire.
Again.
Again.
Again.
The image is almost unbearable.
God speaks.
The king cuts.
God warns.
The king burns.
God calls for repentance.
The king feeds the warning to the flames.
And Scripture records an even darker detail.
Jeremiah 36:24 says:
“Yet neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid, nor did they tear their garments.”
No trembling.
No mourning.
No repentance.
No brokenness.
The scroll burned…
and apparently the king felt safer when the words disappeared.
But destroying the page did not destroy the truth.
And that is where Jehoiakim’s story walks out of an ancient palace and directly into our lives.
Because you do not need a knife to cut the Bible.
You can do it quietly.
You can love:
“God is love.”
And cut:
“Repent.”
You can treasure:
“Judge not.”
While ignoring Christ’s command:
“Go, and sin no more.”
You can celebrate grace while resisting holiness.
You can sing about surrender while secretly protecting the one thing you refuse to surrender.
You can want Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
And suddenly Jehoiakim’s knife does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Sometimes our knife is preference.
Sometimes it is culture.
Sometimes it is politics.
Sometimes it is lust.
Sometimes it is bitterness.
Sometimes it is a relationship we know is pulling us away from Christ.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes it is pride.
Sometimes it is simply this:
“I know what Scripture says…
but I do not want God telling me what to do.”
That sentence can live inside a church pew.
It can sing worship songs.
It can quote Scripture.
It can even run a Christian social-media page.
Religious appearance has never been the same thing as surrender.
And this story becomes even more sobering when you compare Jehoiakim with his father, Josiah.
Years earlier, another book connected with God’s law had been read before King Josiah.
Josiah heard the words…
and tore his clothes.
Jehoiakim heard the words…
and tore the scroll.
One king allowed the Word to break him.
The other tried to break the Word.
That may be one of the most important spiritual questions you ever ask yourself:
When Scripture contradicts me, which one gets cut?
My desires?
Or God’s Word?
When Jesus confronts my pride, do I repent—or reinterpret?
When Scripture exposes my relationship, do I surrender—or search until I find someone willing to tell me what I want to hear?
When the Gospel exposes my secret sin, do I confess it—or defend it?
When Christ commands forgiveness, do I obey—or keep rehearsing why my bitterness is justified?
Because eventually every disciple reaches the place where Jesus says something the flesh does not want to hear.
And that moment reveals whether we merely admire Christ…
or actually follow Him.
Jehoiakim had another problem.
He apparently believed fire could accomplish what rebellion never can:
make God's Word disappear.
It could not.
After the scroll was burned, the LORD spoke again to Jeremiah.
Jeremiah 36:28 records:
“Take another scroll and write on it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.”
Read that slowly.
Take another scroll.
The king had a knife.
God had another scroll.
The king had a fire.
God still had His Word.
Jehoiakim could destroy parchment.
He could not overthrow the One who spoke through His prophet.
Then Jeremiah 36:32 tells us Jeremiah took another scroll, Baruch wrote the words again, and:
“many similar words were added to them.”
What a reversal.
Jehoiakim tried subtraction.
God answered with addition.
The king tried to silence the message.
The message survived the king.
And centuries later, almost nobody remembers Jehoiakim because of the magnificence of his throne.
Millions remember him because Scripture records the day he tried to burn what God had spoken.
The fire went out.
The king died.
The Word remained.
But there is something deeper here than a warning about respecting the Bible.
This story points toward the desperate condition of the human heart.
Because humanity's deepest problem is not merely that we sometimes dislike particular commandments.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We do not merely need better habits.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need rescue.
We need a new heart.
And that is why the Bible does not end with Jeremiah's burning scroll.
The story keeps moving.
Through exile.
Through promises.
Through prophets.
Through generations waiting for redemption.
Until eventually the Word was not merely written on a scroll.
John opens his Gospel with words that still shake the soul:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος
En archē ēn ho Logos.
“In the beginning was the Word…”
Then John 1:14 declares:
Καὶ ὁ Λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho Logos sarx egeneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Jesus Christ came.
Not merely another prophet.
Not merely another moral teacher.
The eternal Son entered human history.
And humanity did something even more horrifying than Jehoiakim did to the scroll.
We rejected Him.
Jehoiakim used a knife.
Human beings used nails.
Jehoiakim threw God's written warning into a fire.
Human beings nailed the incarnate Son of God to a cross.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And placed in a tomb.
For a moment, it looked as though sinful humanity had silenced Him too.
But you cannot bury the Author of life and expect the grave to keep Him.
Jesus rose.
That is the Gospel.
Not that good people finally learned to behave.
Not that broken people repaired themselves.
Not that sinners climbed high enough to reach God.
God came to us.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
The scandal of the cross became the place where grace was displayed.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come home.
The rebellious can repent.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The person who has spent years cutting God's commands out of his life can finally drop the knife.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe there is a verse you avoid because it gets too close.
Maybe there is a conviction you keep drowning beneath entertainment.
Maybe there is a secret browser history nobody knows about.
Maybe there is an affair hidden behind deleted messages.
Maybe there is bitterness you have carried so long that it feels like part of your personality.
Maybe everybody at church thinks you are strong while you know your prayer life has almost disappeared.
Maybe you preach holiness publicly while negotiating with sin privately.
Maybe you still call yourself Christian, but if you are painfully truthful, Jesus has been standing outside rooms in your heart that you refuse to unlock.
And perhaps this article did not find you because you needed another inspirational Christian post.
Perhaps you needed the uncomfortable mercy of being confronted.
Remember Jeremiah 36.
The warning was not given because God had no interest in forgiving them.
The warning came so they might turn…
and God might forgive.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction calls you out of darkness.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide from Jesus until you become worthy.
You will never become worthy enough to purchase grace.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Confess what you have been defending.
Bring into the light what you have been hiding.
Stop cutting away every truth that hurts.
Sometimes the verse that wounds your pride is the very verse God uses to rescue your life.
And if you have fallen badly, remember our theme:
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
Not because repentance is optional.
Jesus Himself called sinners to repentance.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue worshiping our chains.
Paul rejected that distortion of grace.
Grace saves us and begins transforming us.
Your scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Your addiction does not have to write the ending.
Your adultery does not have to write the ending.
Your pornography does not have to write the ending.
Your pride does not have to write the ending.
Your bitterness does not have to write the ending.
Your religious hypocrisy does not have to write the ending.
Your years of running do not have to write the ending.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your past never happened…
but by redeeming sinners who could never redeem themselves.
What have you been cutting out?
What truth do you hope God will stop mentioning?
What command makes your hand reach for the knife?
What sin are you asking Jesus to tolerate instead of forgive and transform?
Do not burn the warning.
Receive the mercy hidden inside it.
Put down the knife.
Open the Word.
And surrender.
Be real.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not judge them.
Pray for them.
We need fewer Christians pretending they have never struggled and more believers pointing struggling people toward Jesus.
It does not.
Not because giving money makes anyone more spiritual. It does not.
Salvation cannot be bought, and the Gospel must never be sold as though grace had a price tag.
Because Jehoiakim teaches us something we cannot afford to forget.
You can cut the page.
You can burn the scroll.
You can silence the preacher.
You can close the Bible.
You can unfollow the account.
You can drown conviction beneath another night of distraction.
But none of those things changes what God has spoken.
The fire eventually dies.
The knife eventually falls from the hand.
Kings eventually become dust.
But the Word of our God stands forever.
And perhaps the most beautiful possibility is this:
You do not have to become another Jehoiakim.
The hand holding the knife can open in surrender.
The heart resisting correction can break in repentance.
The sinner running from God can turn around.
And because Jesus Christ was crucified and risen for sinners, the story that looked destined to end in judgment can become a testimony of grace.
So put down the knife.
Jesus is still calling you home.
The king burned the scroll because he wanted the warning to disappear—but maybe God preserved the story because He never wanted you to.
